screens.title: What you will be able to do
screens.instruction: Check your progress against these outcomes.

content.text: Remember · Name four types of extreme weather from the photos in Extreme weather.
Understand · Identify the blog’s purpose and explain one prediction from the article in the Reading report.
Analyze · Separate the condition, predicted result and supporting evidence in your group’s case.
Apply · Ask and answer one new What if …? question using the second conditional and give a reason.
Evaluate · Check another group’s prediction against p. 142 and support or revise it with one detail.

screens.title: Group A · Lightning at sea
screens.instruction: 3 minutes. In groups of four, assign a reader, evidence finder, recorder and reporter. Use p. 142 and prepare a 30-second report.

activity.prompt: Compare a boat at sea with a submarine underwater. Record three lines: What if …? / What would happen? / Which detail from the article supports your answer?
activity.modelAnswer: If you were underwater in a submarine, you would be safer than in a boat. The article explains that the submarine is below the surface and lightning usually hits the tallest thing.
activity.rubric: Give one condition, one prediction and one relevant detail from p. 142.

screens.title: Group B · A swimmer in a storm
screens.instruction: 3 minutes. In groups of four, assign a reader, evidence finder, recorder and reporter. Use p. 142 and prepare a 30-second report.

content.alt: Group B · A swimmer in a storm
content.caption: Life, p. 142

activity.prompt: Imagine that lightning hits the water near a swimmer. Record three lines: What if …? / What would happen? / Which detail from the article supports your answer?
activity.modelAnswer: If lightning hit the water near you, the electrical energy would spread across the water. The article also says that a swimmer with their head above the water could be struck.
activity.rubric: Give one condition, one prediction and one relevant detail from p. 142.

screens.title: Group C · A car in extreme weather
screens.instruction: 3 minutes. In groups of four, assign a reader, evidence finder, recorder and reporter. Use p. 142 and prepare a 30-second report.

content.alt: Group C · A car in extreme weather
content.caption: Life, p. 142

activity.prompt: Compare rain at normal driving speed with hail in freezing weather when driving fast. Record three lines: What if …? / What would happen? / Which detail from the article supports your answer?
activity.modelAnswer: Rain would not break the glass at normal driving speed. If you drove fast in hail at freezing temperatures, the hail could break the windscreen. The article notes this happens in some places.
activity.rubric: Give one condition, one prediction and one relevant detail from p. 142.

screens.title: Compare the three cases
screens.instruction: Each reporter has 30 seconds. Listeners check the evidence for one other group on p. 142. After each report, the teacher reveals that case’s model and invites one correction.

activity.prompt: Which group’s prediction did you check? Give the evidence and say whether you would keep or revise the prediction.
activity.modelAnswer: I would keep Group C’s prediction. The article distinguishes normal-speed rain from hail in freezing weather when a car is moving fast.
activity.rubric: Name the group, cite a relevant detail and state a verdict.

screens.title: Read for evidence
screens.instruction: Answer individually after the group reports. Return to p. 142 if you need evidence.

activity.prompt: The blog uses science to explain hypothetical situations.
The article says a person in a boat is safer from lightning than someone underwater in a submarine.
The article says hail can damage a windscreen.

screens.title: Hopes and dreams
screens.instruction: Ask a partner a hypothetical question. Follow up with why.

activity.prompt: If you could live anywhere for a year, where would you go and why?
activity.modelAnswer: If I could live anywhere for a year, I’d choose Canada because I’d like to explore its national parks.
activity.rubric: Use an if-clause, a result with would or ’d, and a reason.

screens.title: Interview a nature photographer
screens.instruction: Take turns asking and answering questions.

activity.prompt: Ask two questions using any-. Answer using at least one compound with some- or no-.
activity.modelAnswer: Did you see anything unusual? Yes, I saw something moving near the river. Did anyone photograph it? No, nobody had a camera.
activity.rubric: Use two any- questions and a natural reply with a compound.

screens.title: One small place, two language targets
screens.instruction: Write a short exit ticket.

activity.prompt: Where would you look for nature if you had one hour? Say what someone might find there.
activity.modelAnswer: If I had one hour, I would look in the school garden. Someone might find something surprising under the leaves.
activity.rubric: Include one accurate second conditional and two appropriate indefinite compounds.
